explain.say: A water tower is a big tank held high above a town. The weight of the water pushing down creates pressure in the pipes, so water flows out of your tap without a pump at your house.

faq.q: Why are water towers so tall?
faq.a: Height gives pressure. The water's weight pushes down through the pipes, and the higher the tank, the harder it pushes, so it can reach homes and upper floors.
asks: How does a water tower work?

faq.q: How much pressure does a water tower make?
faq.a: About one bar for every 10 metres of height. A tank 40 metres above the town gives around four bar at ground level, plenty for most homes.
asks: How does height make water pressure?

faq.q: How does water get into a water tower?
faq.a: Pumps push water up into the tank through a pipe, usually running steadily or at night when demand and electricity prices are low. The same pipe often carries the water back out.

faq.q: Why do towns need water towers?
faq.a: Demand swings a lot, peaking in the morning and evening. The tower stores water to cover those peaks, so the pumps and treatment works can run at a steady rate.
asks: What is a water tower for?

faq.q: What happens to a water tower in a power cut?
faq.a: Because the water flows out by gravity, taps keep running for a while even with the pumps off, and there is a store of water ready for fighting fires.
asks: Do water towers work without electricity?

facts: Each 10 metres of water height produces about 1 bar, roughly 100 kilopascals, of pressure at the bottom.
Water pressure depends on the height of the water, not on the width of the tank.

quiz.say: A town wants more water pressure on its hilltop streets. What change to its water tower would help most?
quiz.show: More pressure on hilltop streets needs…

options.show: A wider tank at the same height
options.say: A wider tank at the same height

quiz.why: Pressure depends on the height of the water above the tap, so raising the tank raises the pressure.

wrong.1: A wider tank stores more water but gives the same pressure at the same height.
wrong.2: Colour may change the water temperature, not the pressure.
